say: Picking an algorithm by reputation is guessing. This trains several on the same data, scores them all the same way, and shows you the whole table rather than just the winner.
A customer churn file: two hundred and forty rows, nine features, and a churned column as the label.
It reads the file and proposes a target and a task type. Churned, classification. You can override both.
Then the algorithms. Three is the minimum, because comparing two tells you almost nothing. Three are on by default, and I am adding two more.
And extra trees. Five algorithms, all scored on the same five folds of the same data.
Training. Each one is cross validated rather than scored on a single split, so a model that got a lucky partition does not win by accident.

There is the leaderboard, and XGBoost takes it. But look at the numbers rather than the ribbon: the five scores sit between about zero point eight one and zero point eight five. The winner is ahead by roughly three hundredths.

That gap is narrower than the run-to-run variation inside a single model, which is what the stability column is telling you. Every one of the five reads variable — their fold scores swing by more than three hundredths of a point, which is wider than the gap between first place and last. The honest conclusion on this dataset is that these five algorithms perform about the same, and the choice should be made on training time or interpretability instead.

And the winner's held-out metrics are reported separately from the score that selected it. Cross validation picked XGBoost on weighted F1; accuracy, precision, recall and area under the ROC curve are measured afterwards and shown alongside it, because the number used to choose a model is not the number you should quote for it.
